finding.claim: delete_file calls require_allowed, which is an alias for acl.is_allowed (a boolean predicate). The return value is discarded, so the 'delete' permission is never enforced and any caller can delete any file.
finding.source: Any HTTP client sending DELETE /files/<fid>. The X-Session-User-Verified header can be absent or any value, and the user needs no grant on the file.
finding.sink: del STORE[fid] at views.py:19, the protected delete operation

trace.note: from acl import is_allowed as require_allowed: the predicate is renamed to look like an enforcing guard
f = STORE[fid] loads the resource from the attacker-supplied id
require_allowed(g.user, f, 'delete') returns False but the result is ignored and nothing aborts
is_allowed only returns a bool; it never raises or aborts

finding.guards_checked: The correct guard acl.ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) aborts with 403 and is used in rename_file (views.py:26), but not in delete_file. before_request load_user only sets g.user and does not reject anonymous requests. No other auth decorator or middleware exists.

verdict.guard_found: none effective: require_allowed (alias of acl.is_allowed, views.py:4) only returns a bool and its result is discarded at views.py:18; load_user (views.py:10-12) only sets g.user and never rejects; the real guard ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) is used only in rename_file (views.py:26).
verdict.reason: views.py:18 calls the bool-returning alias require_allowed (views.py:4 → acl.py:4-5) as a bare statement with no abort, so views.py:19 `del STORE[fid]` runs for any unauthenticated caller who supplies an existing fid.
